notes: Academic prison property JR; Moses J dismissed with nominal costs after parole release.

enrichment.short_title: Fernie v Lincolnshire Police: academic judicial review over seized documents
key_facts: Mr Fernie, a prisoner, sought recovery of documents held by Lincolnshire Police and challenged magistrates' handling of related proceedings.
By the hearing he had been released on parole and the police agreed to return the property.
Blackburne J had granted permission on the basis there was a strongly arguable case that magistrates wrongly refused an adjournment when Mr Fernie failed to attend.
Disputed issues included whether police retention complied with the code and whether the code was consistent with statute.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of magistrates' proceedings concerning property held by the Chief Constable of Lincolnshire Police.
enrichment.outcome: Proceedings dismissed as academic because the property would be returned and Mr Fernie was on parole; the court ordered the respondents to pay £100 towards his costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where judicial review has become wholly academic because the claimant has been released and the disputed property will be returned, the court should not decide substantive issues about police retention powers or magistrates' adjournment practice.
legal_issues: Whether the judicial review remained live after the claimant's release and agreement to return property
Whether magistrates erred in refusing an adjournment when the prisoner did not attend
Whether police retention of documents complied with statutory and code requirements

notes: Detailed GCC chiropractic publicity appeal; all grounds failed but suspension never took effect.

enrichment.short_title: Gage v General Chiropractic Council: misleading clinic booklet and suspension appeal

statutes_considered.title: National Health Service Reform and Health Care Professions Act 2002

key_facts: Dr Gage distributed a promotional booklet containing patient success stories suggesting chiropractic could treat MS, cataracts and Parkinson's disease.
The General Chiropractic Council's Professional Conduct Committee found multiple breaches of the Chiropractors Code and CAP Code and imposed suspension until 31 October 2004.
Dr Brown's expert report was obtained at investigation stage but not disclosed to Dr Gage until the PCC hearing.
Dr Gage appealed under section 31, suspending the sanction until disposal of the appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal by rehearing from a General Chiropractic Council Professional Conduct Committee suspension order.
enrichment.outcome: All eight grounds of appeal were dismissed, but because the suspension order ended on 31 October 2004 while the appeal remained pending under section 31(2), Dr Gage never served any period of suspension; costs ordered at 80% in favour of the GCC.
enrichment.ratio: Investigating committees must disclose significant expert evidence to chiropractors under investigation; breach of paragraph 8.4 does not require a finding of dishonesty; a suspension framed to end on a fixed date rather than for a specified period may expire before it can begin if an appeal under section 31 remains undetermined.
legal_issues: Whether non-disclosure of Dr Brown's report required the PCC proceedings to be stayed
Whether the PCC applied the correct civil standard of proof
Whether success stories breached the CAP Code and Chiropractors Code
Whether the suspension order was lawful and its effect where an appeal was pending

enrichment.short_title: Wickramaratna v Cambridge: High Court Master civil restraint order jurisdiction
key_facts: Ms Wickramaratna sought injunctions and transfer of county court proceedings after a disputed Cambridge Chemistry Department studentship.
Master Fontaine struck out her High Court claim in her absence on 9 October 2003 and barred further applications without leave.
The claimant had been hospitalised and detained under the Mental Health Act when the Master made the order.
She abandoned her application to set aside the order before MacKay J, who refused to entertain a fresh application without permission.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal on permission limited to whether a High Court Master had power to make a Grepe v Loam / limited civil restraint order in October 2003.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; a High Court Master had jurisdiction to make a limited civil restraint order because it is a regulatory case-management direction, not an injunction within CPR Part 2 Practice Direction paragraph 2.
enrichment.ratio: A civil restraint order protecting the court process from abuse is not an injunction for CPR Part 2 purposes and may be made by a High Court Master; a litigant cannot insist on having applications heard by a judge rather than a Master.
legal_issues: Whether a High Court Master could make a Grepe v Loam order before CPR Part 3 Practice Direction 3C
Whether the order was an injunction requiring a judge
Whether the claimant needed permission before making further applications

notes: Brighton street fight appeal; conviction safe despite propensity direction flaw; sentence reduced.

enrichment.short_title: R v Morris: summing-up challenge and section 18 sentence after ear-biting assault
key_facts: After a night out in Brighton, Nathan Hunt had part of his ear bitten off during a confrontation with the appellant Jess Morris and his girlfriend.
The Crown case was an unprovoked attack; the defence was self-defence after Nathan and Simon Annis pursued and assaulted Morris.
Morris had spent 1994 dishonesty convictions introduced at trial after attacking prosecution witnesses' character.
He was convicted of wounding with intent and common assault and sentenced to five years' imprisonment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal criminal appeal against conviction and sentence by leave of Bean J after a five-day Lewes Crown Court trial.
enrichment.outcome: Conviction appeal dismissed as safe; sentence on count 1 reduced from five years to three-and-a-half years as manifestly excessive for a spur-of-the-moment section 18 offence.
enrichment.ratio: Where a defendant with spent dishonesty convictions is not treated as of good character, the judge should still give a modified propensity direction, but failure to do so may not render a conviction unsafe if character evidence sufficiently addressed likelihood of violence; detailed summing-up criticisms must be assessed cumulatively and against the jury's standard caveat.
legal_issues: Whether the judge's summing-up was biased or materially defective
Whether a propensity limb good character direction was required for spent dishonesty convictions
Whether five years was manifestly excessive for wounding with intent

enrichment.short_title: Soteriou v Ultrachem: illegality and Article 6 in sham self-employment claim
key_facts: Mr Soteriou sued Ultrachem Ltd for breach of contract after his employment relationship ended.
An employment tribunal found he had been the prime mover in preserving sham self-employment and making fraudulent statements to tax investigators.
The tribunal held it would be against public policy to allow him to claim employee benefits.
The deputy judge held the tribunal findings operated as issue estoppel and the contract was unenforceable for illegality.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal application for permission to appeal from a deputy High Court judge upholding strike-out on illegality and issue estoppel grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; no important point of principle warranted a second appeal given the tribunal's factual findings and domestic illegality analysis.
enrichment.ratio: Where a claimant actively participated in a dishonest tax arrangement, domestic contract illegality may bar enforcement even without relying on the illegal act; Article 6 is not engaged because illegality defines the content of the right rather than denying access to court.
legal_issues: Whether employment tribunal illegality findings bound subsequent civil proceedings
Whether the claimant had to rely on illegal conduct to enforce the contract
Whether Article 6, Article 1 Protocol 1 or Article 14 ECHR prevented the illegality defence

notes: Police witness anonymity at inquest; Article 2 threshold and Saville guidance applied.

enrichment.short_title: Bennett inquest: anonymity for police officers who shot Derek Bennett
key_facts: Derek Bennett was shot dead by Officer A, accompanied by Officer B, in July 2001; the CPS decided no prosecution should be brought.
The coroner refused anonymity for the two sergeants at the inquest despite evidence of threats linked to a local Rastafarian temple.
Mitting J quashed the coroner's decision and directed anonymity including screens and video-link evidence.
The deceased's family appealed, arguing the coroner correctly applied a serious-possibility threshold test.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal against a judicial review quashing a coroner's refusal to grant witness anonymity at an inquest.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Article 2 was engaged and the coroner erred in applying too high a threshold and in failing to give weight to local police risk assessments.
enrichment.ratio: For anonymity at an inquest the threefold Saville test applies; Article 2 is engaged where there are reasonable grounds objectively justifying a witness's fears for life, not only where there is a real and immediate Osman-level risk.
legal_issues: The correct threshold for engaging Article 2 on anonymity applications
Whether the coroner's factual assessment of threat evidence was irrational
Whether the judge could substitute his own decision rather than remit to the coroner

enrichment.short_title: Wall v Brighton: planning permission quashed for absent summary reasons

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (General Development Procedure) Order 1995

key_facts: Brighton and Hove granted permission to demolish Ruston house and build eight flats at Withdean Avenue.
Neighbour Mrs Wall of No 6 Lions Gardens objected to overlooking and overshadowing from the closer northern elevation.
The decision notice listed relevant policies but contained no summary reasons for granting permission as required from 6 December 2003.
After judicial review was issued, councillors were asked five months later to recall their reasons by letter.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a planning permission granted by Brighton and Hove City Council on 18 March 2004.
enrichment.outcome: Ground 1 (failure to consider impact on No 6) failed; ground 2 succeeded and the planning permission was quashed for breach of article 22(1)(a).
enrichment.ratio: Article 22(1)(a) requires summary reasons in the decision notice itself to inform the public and discipline committee decision-making; post hoc private correspondence with councillors cannot cure a complete absence of reasons, unlike EIA post-grant disclosure requirements.
legal_issues: Whether the committee failed to consider the amenity impact on the closest neighbouring bungalow
Whether absence of summary reasons in the decision notice rendered the grant unlawful
Whether ex post councillor statements could save the notice

enrichment.short_title: A-G Ref No 96 of 2004: unduly lenient park robbery by Martin Keenan
key_facts: Martin Keenan attacked three strangers in Stockport's Hollywood Park after a snooker club outing, punching one victim and beating another with a bar or cue.
Ian Minshull suffered permanent hand deformity defending his head and lost his nursing course; property including a phone and chain was stolen.
Keenan pleaded guilty to robbery, section 20 wounding and section 47 assault and received three years on the lead count.
He had prior robbery convictions and was recently off licence when the offences occurred on the eve of his 21st birthday.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the 1988 Act against an unduly lenient Crown Court sentence.
enrichment.outcome: Reference allowed; the robbery sentence was increased from three years to three years and nine months with concurrent terms on other counts unchanged.
enrichment.ratio: Night-time park robberies with weapons, gratuitous violence, multiple victims and prior robbery convictions ordinarily merit about five years; a modest uplift may still be warranted where mitigation was overstated but double jeopardy and genuine remorse counsel against a large increase.
legal_issues: Whether three years was unduly lenient for robbery with weapon and permanent injury
Application of Lord Woolf's mobile-phone robbery sentencing guidance
Whether this marginal dispute warranted an Attorney General's reference

enrichment.short_title: DPP v Baker: six-month limit and background evidence in harassment prosecution
key_facts: Margaret Baker was prosecuted for harassing Suzanne Brown, wife of her former partner, by letters and calls over nearly three years.
Magistrates excluded pre-October 2002 incidents as outside the six-month summary limitation period.
The relationship background included anonymous calls, letters about the affair, and repeated encounters in Hexham.
Both prosecution and defence agreed the exclusion ruling was wrong.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal by case stated from magistrates' acquittal on a section 2 Protection from Harassment Act charge.
enrichment.outcome: The magistrates erred in excluding earlier conduct, but the court declined to remit for rehearing given the lapse of time and minimal recent incidents.
enrichment.ratio: Harassment is a continuing offence complete only when the last act occurs, so earlier conduct within the charged course may be admissible if at least one act falls within section 127; background evidence is also admissible under Pettman/Williams to prove authorship, intent and non-coincidence.
legal_issues: Whether pre-limitation harassment incidents were admissible in a continuing course-of-conduct charge
Whether excluded evidence was background material under R v Pettman
Whether the case should be remitted for rehearing

enrichment.short_title: Matin v Attorney General: child welfare and contempt proceedings after court fracas
key_facts: A heated confrontation occurred outside Court 32 after Singer J's residence hearing in long-running proceedings over Forhad Matin.
The Attorney General sought a declaration that contempt proceedings against Dr Pelling would not harm the child before pursuing conduct contempt.
The President granted the declaration in July 2003 on the mistaken assumption Forhad living with his father meant he need not know about the case.
Forhad would inevitably be a front-line witness if conduct contempt proceedings continued.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal on permission to appeal against a President's declaration under Re M (Contact Order: Committal) principles.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted; appeal allowed and the declaration set aside; the court exercised its own discretion to refuse a fresh declaration ending conduct contempt proceedings while publication contempt proceedings remained.
enrichment.ratio: Under Re M, a declaration whether contempt proceedings would harm a child must be exercised on accurate facts about the child's likely involvement; where a child would be a necessary witness, assuming insulation from the proceedings is an erroneous basis for authorising committal.
legal_issues: Whether the President erred in assuming the child would not be involved in contempt proceedings
Whether oral evidence should have been heard on the declaration application
Whether the court should remit or exercise its own discretion afresh
